Section.Description: Lethal concentration is the estimated concentration of a chemical expected to cause death in a test subject. It is usually expressed as the median lethal concentration (LC50), which is the estimated concentration of a chemical expected to cause death in 50% of the test subjects. There are also other measures such as LC0 (no deaths) and LC100 (all deaths).

Lethal dose values describe the amount of a chemical expected to cause death in test subjects under specified exposure conditions. These values are commonly expressed as dose-based toxicity endpoints such as the median lethal dose (LD50), which represents the estimated dose expected to cause death in 50% of the test subjects. Other endpoints include LD0 (no observed deaths) and LD100 (death in all test subjects).

Effect level values describe the dose or exposure level of a chemical associated with observed biological or toxicological effects in test subjects. These dose-based endpoints include Low Effect Level (LEL), No Effect Level (NEL), Lowest Observed Effect Level (LOEL), No Observed Effect Level (NOEL), Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL), and No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL), which represent exposure levels associated with observed or unobserved effects or adverse effects under specified exposure conditions.

Screening levels are health- or environment-based threshold values used to identify chemical concentrations or doses that may warrant additional evaluation or risk assessment. Examples include Ecological Screening Levels (ESLs), Soil Screening Levels (SSLs), Health-Based Screening Levels (HBSLs), and Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for drinking water.

Reference and risk values are derived toxicity benchmarks used to evaluate potential human health risks associated with chemical exposure. These values are typically developed from experimental toxicity data together with uncertainty or safety factors. Examples include Reference Dose (RfD), Reference Concentration (RfC), Derived No-Effect Level (DNEL), and other health-based guidance or risk assessment values.

Military Exposure Guidelines (MEGs) are established by the Department of Defense (DoD) to evaluate and manage chemical and environmental health risks during deployments. MEGs help determine how chemical exposures in air, water, and soil could impact a service member's health and mission readiness

Medium-specific concentration (MSC) is a chemical concentration in a specific medium (e.g., air, water, soil) that is considered to be safe for human health or the environment.  MSCs are used in risk assessments to evaluate potential risks from chemical exposures in different media.  The MSCs for a chemical can be derived from various sources, such as regulatory standards, toxicity data, and risk assessment models.

StringWithMarkup.String: /CASE REPORTS/ A pesticide poisoning victim suspected initially as having died a natural death was autopsied. The victim was a 47-year-old male. Macroscopically, signs of acute death and, in particular, general erosion in the mucosa of the airways and esophagus were observed. In the gastric contents, which had a pungent smell and a greenish-brown color, 5.00 g/L of propanil, 1.27 g/L of carbaryl, 0.38 g/L of ethylbenzene, and 0.32 g/L of xylene were detected. In the blood (serum), 21.6 mg/L of propanil, 8.1 mg/L of carbaryl, 1.7 mg/L of ethylbenzene, and 4.0 mg/L of xylene were identified. Postmortem methemoglobinemia (45%) was recognized. The cause of death was considered to have been pesticide poisoning; propanil was probably most responsible for his death. The police considered the case to be "death with illness as the suspected cause." By performing an autopsy, however, we were able to clarify that the cause of death was pesticide poisoning.

StringWithMarkup.String: Propanil's production may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams; its use as a herbicide will result in its direct release to the environment. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 9.08X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates propanil will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase propanil will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 4.2 days. Particulate-phase propanil will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. Propanil was susceptible to photolysis by sunlight in water and on soil surfaces, and may also be susceptible to direct photolysis in air. If released to soil, propanil is expected to have high to low mobility based upon Koc values of 141 to 800. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 1.7X10-9 atm-cu m/mole. Utilizing the Japanese MITI test, 21.1% of the theoretical BOD was reached in 4 weeks indicating that biodegradation may be an important environmental fate process in soil. Other soil studies indicate as much as 99% degradation in 15 days. If released into water, propanil is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the Koc values. Biodegradation half-lives were reported as 17 hours to 6 days in aqueous environments. Volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. A BCF of 1.6 suggests bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Hydrolysis is not expected based upon a study where propanil was stable in distilled water at 20 °C and pHs 6-9 for more than four months. Occupational exposure to propanil may occur through inhalation and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where propanil is produced or used. Exposure of the general population to propanil may occur through inhalation and dermal contact resulting from aerial spraying nearby. Propanil is not registered for residential use and may not be used in or around public buildings, schools, or recreational areas where children could be exposed. (SRC)

StringWithMarkup.String: The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of propanil with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals has been estimated as 3.8X10-12 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) using a structure estimation method(1). After irradiation in the photoreactor for 34 days, 18% of a 200 mg/L solution of propanil in distilled water remained unchanged(3). A 100 mg/L solution of propanil degraded 50% in 4 hrs when irradiated with 300 nm sunlight lamps(4). Half-lives for the photolysis of propanil by sunlight of 60.3, 55.4, 57.3, 40.3, and 44.1 days were reported in lake water, river water, marine water, ground water, and distilled water, respectively(5). Half-lives for the photolysis of propanil on soil surfaces of 21.1, 19.9, and 18.4 days were reported using sandy clay loam, clay loam, and sandy loam soils, respectively(5).

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.

StringWithMarkup.String: Occupational exposure to propanil may occur through inhalation and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where propanil is produced or used(SRC). In pesticide formulating plants, exposure to pesticides, like propanil, may be from spillage; furthermore, there is a potential for dermal exposure and inhalation at mixing and bagging stations(2). Propanil is applied to several crops via aerial or ground spraying(1,3). Crop workers may be exposed during application; however, their main exposure results from contact with treated foliage or to pesticide or pesticide-contaminated material made airborne through agitation of foliage during work activity(2). Incidental to treating a crop, some pesticides, such as propanil, may drift onto workers in neighboring fields or in nearby suburban areas without there being any intent to treat those areas(2,3). Propanil is not registered for residential use and may not be used in or around public buildings, schools, or recreational areas where children might be exposed(4). The general population may be exposed to propanil through consumption of contaminated foods(5,6). After aerial application to rice fields in Arkansas, propanil was detected 1,000 m from the fields at a concn range of 5-52 ug/100 sq cm on denim/gauze patches measuring potential dermal exposure during and after aerial application(3). Individuals living near a rice field aerially treated with propanil are potentially exposed to propanil; wind speed and direction are important factors influencing the concentration of aerially applied pesticides(7). Exposure of the general population to propanil may occur through inhalation and dermal contact resulting from spraying nearby areas(SRC).
